items.meta_title: Self-Signed or Trusted Certificate on a VPN Server | VpnHood!
items.meta_description: What your VPN server's certificate tells a network: why a trusted one is best, and why a plain self-signed one can beat an invalid one naming a real site.
items.title: Which certificate should your server use?
items.lead: Anyone who connects to your server sees its certificate, so one probe can give the server away. Use a trusted certificate if you can. If you cannot, an honest self-signed certificate can still be better than a false one.
items.compare_title: What each certificate tells a network
items.kind_trusted_sees: A valid certificate for your domain, signed by a certificate authority.
items.kind_trusted_looks: It looks like an ordinary website or service.
items.kind_self_sees: A certificate no authority signed, with a made-up name, as on a new server.
items.kind_self_looks: It looks like a private server, such as a router or a test machine.
items.kind_invalid_sees: A self-signed certificate that names a real site, at an address that is not that site's.
items.kind_invalid_looks: It looks like a server pretending to be something it is not.
items.invalid_both: A browser rejects both. The difference is what each one claims.
items.invalid_self: A made-up name claims nothing, so there is nothing to disprove. Routers, test machines and private tools show the same kind of certificate every day, and a network that blocks them all cuts those off too.
items.invalid_false: A real site's name is a claim anyone can check: that site has a certificate from an authority and addresses of its own, and your server has neither. No ordinary server does that, so blocking it costs a network nothing.
items.invalid_when: A real site's name can still help on a network that goes by the name alone, where it can pass and a made-up name cannot. To try it, add one on a managed server or on a standalone server.
items.invalid_dress: There is no point dressing up a self-signed certificate. Its organization, how long it lasts and its extensions change nothing, as a probe sees at once that no authority signed it.
items.domain_title: Get a domain if you can
items.domain_cost: A trusted certificate is the real answer to a probe, and it costs little: a domain is cheap, and Let's Encrypt's certificates are free.
items.domain_host: Use a host of the domain, such as [domain_api_example]. Many sites keep an API or their files on a host of their own that refuses strangers, as your server does, so it looks ordinary. [domain_www_example] stays yours for any site you like, on any hosting.
items.domain_limit: A domain does not get your users past a blocked address, though, as it leads to the same server. Only a reverse proxy does that.
